name: Philippus of Thessalonica
bio: Philippus of Thessalonica compiled the Garland that continued Meleager's, collecting the epigrams of poets of the Augustan age and after, and wrote epigrams of his own. Paton's index puts him in the second century AD; the editor follows the more usual first-century date.
This archive files under his name every epigram that Paton heads “Philippus”, including Book IV, 2, his proem to the Garland.

poems.title: Book IV, 2: The Stephanus of Philippus
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Plucking for thee flowers of Helicon and the firstborn blooms of the famous Pierian forests, reaping the ears of a newer page, I have in my turn plaited a garland to be like that of Meleager. Thou knowest, excellent Camillus, the famous writers of old; learn to know the less abundant verses of our younger ones. Antipater will beautify the garland like an ear of corn, Crinugoras like a cluster of ivy-berries ; Antiphilus shall shine like a bunch of grapes, Tullius like melilot and Philodemus like amaracus, Parmenion like myrtle and Antiphanes like a rose ; Automedon is ivy, Zonas a lily, Bianor oak-leaves, Antigonus olive leaves, and Diodorus a violet. You may compare Evenus to a laurel, and many others whom I have inwoven to what freshly flowered blooms you like.

poems.title: Book VI, 5
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Piso the fisherman, weighed down by long toil and his right hand already shaky, gives to Hermes these his rods with the lines hanging from their tips, his oar that swam through the sea, his curved hooks whose points bite the fishes’ throats, his net fringed with lead, the float that announced where his weel lay, his two wicker creels, the flint pregnant with fire that sets the tinder alight, and his anchor, the trap that holds fast wandering ships.

poems.title: Book VI, 36
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: These trusses from the furrows of his little field did Sosicles the husbandman dedicate to thee, Demeter, who lovest the corn ; for this isa rich harvest of grain he hath gathered. But another time, too, may he bring back his sickle blunted by reaping.

poems.title: Book VI, 38
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: To thee Poseidon, Lord of the sea, did Amyntichus give these his last gifts, when he ceased from his toil on the deep—his nets edged with lead that plunge into the sea, his oar still drunk with the brine, his spear for killing sea-monsters, strong lance of the waters, his weel ever betrayed by floats, his anchor, firm hand of his boat, and the flint, dear to sailors, that has the art of guarding the seed of fire.

poems.title: Book VI, 62
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Callimenes, on giving up his work, now old age has veiled his eyes, dedicates to the Muses his circular lead which marks off the margin of the pages, and the knife that sharpens his pointed pens, his longest ruler, and the pumice from the beach, the dry porous stone of the sea.

poems.title: Book VI, 90
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Poseidon, King of the sea, to thee doth Archides, now he hath ceased to wander along the beach, dedicate his anchor that rests in the seaweed and secures his boat, his two oars that repel the water, the leads over which his net forms a vault, his weels marked by floats, his broad-brimmed rainproof hat, and the flint that generates light for mariners at even.

poems.title: Book VI, 92
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Demophon the goldsmith, his eyes misty with age, dedicates to Hermes the windy bellows of his forge, the keen-biting file that scrapes the gold, the doubleclawed fire-tongs, and these hare’s pads that gather up the shavings.

poems.title: Book VI, 94
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Clytosthenes, his feet that raced in fury now enfeebled by age, dedicates to thee, Rhea of the lion-car, his tambourines beaten by the hand, his shrill hollow-rimmed cymbals, his double-flute that calls through its horn, on which he once made shrieking music, twisting his neck about, and the two-edged knife with which he opened his veins.

poems.title: Book VI, 99
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Philoxenides the worthy goatherd dedicated thee, the Pan he carved from an unbarked beech trunk, after sacrificing an old he-goat and making thy holy altar drunk with the first milk of a she-goat. In reward for which the goats in his fold shall all bear twins in the womb and escape the sharp tooth of the wolf.

poems.title: Book VI, 101
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Timasion, whose limbs have now lost their lustiness, dedicated to thee, slow-footed Hephaestus, his knives that have slaughtered many beasts, his windy bellows that feed the fire, his pierced tammy and that four-footed bridge of fire, the charcoal pan on which the meat is set, his ladle that skims off the foaming fat, together with his iron-fingered flesh-hook.

poems.title: Book VI, 102
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: To thee, Priapus, who lovest the wayfarer, did the gardener Lamon, praying that his trees and his own limbs may flourish, dedicate a yellow-coated pomegranate, figs wrinkled like old men, half-ripe reddening grapes plucked from a cluster, a sweet-scented quince with a fleece of fine down, a walnut peeping from its green outer skin, a cucumber wont to lie embedded in its leaves with the bloom on it, and a goldensmocked olive already ripe.

poems.title: Book VI, 103: Imitation of No. 205
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Leontichus, when time had stripped from his limbs all bloom, gave to thee, grey-eyed Athene, his taut plumb-line weighted with lead, his hammer that strikes planks, his curved bow-drill with its string attached to it at both ends, his sturdy axe for hewing tree-trunks, his straight-running saw that follows the drops of red ochre, his augers worked by the hand, his gimlets, and his taut ochre-stained line just touched by the extreme edge of the rule.

poems.title: Book VI, 104
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Lysrxenus, deprived of the use of his limbs by much ploughing, suspends to Demeter with the wreath of corn, his seed-bag carried on the shoulder, his mallet for breaking clods, his curved sickle that gathers the corn, his sharp-toothed threshing “trebbia,” his plough-tree with the curved plough and the share that loves the earth, his goad that pricks the oxen in the rear, the traces attached to their legs that make them turn, and his wooden winnowing-fork, the hand of the husbandman.

poems.title: Book VI, 107
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: The huntsman Gelo dedicates to Pan, the ranger of the forest, me, his spear, the edge of which time hath worn by use, also the old rags of his twisted hunting-nets, his nooses that throttle the neck, his foot-traps, made of sinews, quick to nip beasts by the leg, and the collars, masters of his dogs’ necks; for Time has overcome his strength, and he has now renounced wandering over the hills.

poems.title: Book VI, 114
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: We hang in the porch, a gift of the king to Heracles, the skin and mighty horns, fourteen palms long, of a wild bull, which when it confronted Philip, glorying in its strength, his terrible spear brought to ground, on the spurs of Orbelus, the land of wild cattle. Blest indeed is Macedon, which is ruled by such a chief.

poems.title: Book VI, 231
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Queen of black-soiled Egypt, goddess with the linen robe, come to my well-appointed sacrifice. On the wood ashes a crumbling cake is laid for thee and there is a white pair of water-haunting geese, and powdery nard round many-grained figs, and wrinkled raisins and sweet-scented frankincense. But if, O queen, thou savest Damis from poverty, as thou didst from the deep, he will sacrifice a kid with gilded horns.

poems.title: Book VI, 236
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: See how the brazen beaks, voyage-loving weapons of ships, here preserved as relics of the fight at Actium, shelter, like a hive, the waxy gift of the bees, weighted all round by the humming swarm. Beneficent indeed is the righteous rule of Caesar; he hath taught the arms of the enemy to bear the fruits of peace, not war.

poems.title: Book VI, 240
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Archer daughter of Zeus and Leto, Artemis, watcher of wild creatures, who dwellest in the recesses of the hills, this very day send the hated sickness from our bestof emperors forth even unto the Hyperboreans. For Philippus will offer o’er thy altars smoke of frankincense, sacrificing a mountain boar.

poems.title: Book VI, 247
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Patitantian Maid who lovest the loom,” Aesione, now bowed with age, suspends to thee the gift of her poverty, her weaving-comb that sings like the early-chattering swallows, with the prongs of which weaver Pallas smooths the thread, her comb for dressing the wool, her spindle worn by the fingers, swimming () with the twirling thread, and her wicker basket which the wool dressed by her teeth once filled.

poems.title: Book VI, 251
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Phoebus, who dwellest on the sheer height of Leucas visible from afar to sailors, and washed by the lonian sea, accept from the seamen a feast of barley cake kneaded by the hand, and a libation mixed in a small cup, the poor light too of this lamp, imbibed by its half-satisfied mouth from a parsimonious oil-flask. In return for which be kind to us, and send to our sails a favourable breeze carrying us with it to the shore of Actium.

poems.title: Book VI, 259
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: A. Who set thee up, the beardless Hermes, by the starting point of the course? &. Hermogenes. A. Whose son? B. Daimenes’. A. From whence? B. From Antioch. A. Why did he honour thee? B. As his helper in the race. A. What race? . At Isthmus and Nemea. A. He ranthere, then? B. Yes, and came in first. A. Whom did he beat? JB. Nine other boys, and he flew as if he had my feet.

poems.title: Book VII, 186
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: But now the sweet flute was echoing in the bridal chamber of Nikippis, and the house rejoiced in the clapping of hands at her wedding. But the voice of wailing burst in upon the bridal hymn, and we saw her dead, the poor child, not yet quite a wife. O tearful Hades, why didst thou divorce the bridegroom and bride, thou who thyself takest delight in ravishment?

poems.title: Book VII, 187
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Aged Nico garlanded the tomb of maiden Melite. Hades, was thy judgement righteous?

poems.title: Book VII, 234
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Aquius, the bold captain, whose neck was hung with the golden torques he had won in the wars, when crippled by wasting disease, ran back in his mind to the history of his past deeds of valour, and drove his sword into his vitals, saying but this: “Men perish by the sword, cowards by disease.”

poems.title: Book VII, 362
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Here the sarcophagus holds the holy head of good Aetius, the distinguished orator. To the house of Hades went his body, but his soul in Olympus rejoices with Zeus and the other gods . . .; but neither eloquence nor God can make man immortal.

poems.title: Book VII, 382
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Thou gavest me up dead to the land, cruel sea, and now thou carriest off the little remnant of my ashes. I alone am shipwrecked even in Hades, and not even on land shall I cease to be dashed on the dreadful rocks. Either bury me, hiding (?) me in thy waters, or if thou givest me up to the land, steal not a corpse that now belongs to the land.

poems.title: Book VII, 383
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Look on this corpse of a most unhappy man scattered on the beach shredded by the sea-dashed rocks. Here lies the hairless and toothless head and here the five fingers of a hand, here the fleshless ribs, the feet without their sinews and the disjointed legs. This man of many parts once was one. Blest indeed are those who were never born to see the sun!

poems.title: Book VII, 385
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Hero Protesilaus, for that thou didst first initiate Ilion into looking on the wrath of Grecian spears, the tall trees also that grow round thy tomb are all big with hatred of Troy. If from their topmost branches they see Ilion, they wither and cast off the beauty of their foliage. How great was thy boiling wrath against Troy, if tree-trunks preserve the spite thou didst bear thy foes.

poems.title: Book VII, 394
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: The miller possessed me also during his life, the deep-voiced revolving stone, the wheat-crushing servant of fertile Demeter, and on his death he set me up on this tomb, an emblem of his calling. So he finds me ever heavy, in his work while he lived, and now he is dead, on his bones.

poems.title: Book VII, 405
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Avoid, O stranger, this terrible tomb of Hipponax, which hails forth verses, Hipponax whose very ashes ery in iambics his hatred of Bupalus, lest thou wake the sleeping wasp, who not even in Hades has lulled his spite to rest, but in a halting measure launcheth straight shafts of song.

poems.title: Book VII, 554
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: The mason Architeles with mourning hands constructed a tomb for Agathanor his son, Alas alas! this stone no chisel cut, but drenched by many tears it crumbled. Thou, tablet, rest lightly on the dead, that he may say “Of a truth it was my father’s hand which placed this stone on me.”

poems.title: Book IX, 11
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: One man was maimed in his legs, while another had lost his eyesight, but each contributed to the other that of which mischance had deprived him. For the blind man, taking the lame man on his shoulders, kept a straight course by listening to the other’s orders. It was bitter, all-daring necessity which taught them all this, instructing them how, by dividing their imperfections between them, to make a perfect whole.

poems.title: Book IX, 22
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: The temple servants destined as an acceptable sacrifice to Latona’s daughter a heifer big with young; but happy birth-pangs anticipated her approaching death, and she was sent to the herd to bear her child in freedom. For the goddess who presides over child-bed deemed it not right to slay creatures in labour, having learnt to pity them.

poems.title: Book IX, 56
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: The child, treading on the frozen stream of Thracian Hebrus, did not escape death; but when he slipped into the river, now less solidly frozen, his tender neck was cut through by the ice. The rest of his body was carried away, but the head which remained on the ice gave of necessity cause for a funeral. Unhappy she whose offspring was divided between fire and water and seeming to belong to both, belongs not wholly to either.

poems.title: Book IX, 83
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: The dolphins, the fish-eating dogs of the sea, were sporting round the ship as she moved rapidly on her course. A boar-hound, taking them for game, dashed, poor fellow, into the sea, as he would have dashed on land. He perished for the sake of a chase that was strange to him; for not all dogs are light of foot in the sea.

poems.title: Book IX, 85
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: The sea destroyed my boat, but Heaven bestowed on me, as I was carried hither and thither, a more welcome natural boat. For seeing my father’s body coming to me opportunely, I climbed on it, a solitary oarsman, a burden which it was its duty to bear. The old man bore me to the harbour, thus giving life to me twice, on land as a babe and again at sea.

poems.title: Book IX, 88
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: I, the honey-voiced nightingale, was flying over the sea, complaining of Boreas (for not even the wind that blows from Thrace is kind to me), when a dolphin received me on his back, the sea-creature serving as the chariot of the winged one. Borne by this most faithful boatman, I charmed the oarless sailor by the lyre of my lips. The dolphins ever served as oarsmen to the Muses without payment. The tale of Arion is not untrue.

poems.title: Book IX, 89
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Ancient Nico, fending off distressful famine, was gleaning the ears of corn with the girls, and perished from the heat. Her fellow-labourers piled up for her a woodless funeral pyre from the straw of the corn. Be not wrathful, Demeter, if the maidens clothed a child of Earth in the fruits of the earth.

poems.title: Book IX, 232
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: I am the neck of an Adriatic wine-jar, once honeyvoiced when I bore in my belly the gift of Bacchus. But now I am broken I stand here as a strong support for a newly-planted vine which reaches up to climb over this delicate arbour. Ever do I serve Bacchus; either I guard him faithfully in his old age, or rear him in his youth.

poems.title: Book IX, 240
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: A ram with crumpled horns was rushing fiercely to butt Calyptra’s little boy, who had strayed from his mother, when the boar of Heracles, breaking his tether, buried his tusks in the ram’s belly and gave the child its life. Is it because he remembers Hera’s cruelty that Heracles pities children of tender age?

poems.title: Book IX, 247
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: I am a fine plane-tree that the furious blasts of the south wind uprooted and laid low on the ground. But after a bath of wine I stand again erect, vivified both in summer and winter by a rain sweeter than that of heaven. By death I lived, and I alone, after drinking the juice of Bacchus which makes others bend, am seen to stand straighter.

poems.title: Book IX, 253
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Splendid in Thebes was the marriage of Cadmus, but that of Oedipus was abominable. Bacchus welcomed the orgies which Pentheus, having ridiculed, bewailed. The walls arose to the music of strings, but groaned as they crumbled to the flute’s. Holy were the birth-pangs of Antiope, but Iocasta’s heavy with doom. Ino loved her child, but Athamas was impious. The city was always famous (?). See how for good or evil History always had plenty to tell of Thebes.

poems.title: Book IX, 254
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: I, Pumaents, who bore children but to feed the funeral pyre, the mother weighed down by grief, who had seen the burial of three, sought refuge in the fruit of another womb; for, indeed, was confident that the son I had not borne myself would live. So, though I had given birth to so many, I brought up an adopted son. But Fate would not allow me to possess even the gift of another mother; for no sooner was he called mine than he died, and now I have become a cause of mourning even to other mothers.

poems.title: Book IX, 255
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Nerepy Aristides reckoned his possessions as great ; his one sheep was a flock, his one cow a herd. But he lost both ; a wolf killed the ewe, and the cow died in calving. So that the stock of his poor farm was gone, and the luckless man, noosing his neck in the strap of his wallet, perished by his shed that no longer echoed to the sound of bleating.

poems.title: Book IX, 262
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: A. once counted Aristodice to be a proud mother, for six times had she been delivered of her womb’s burden. But water vied with earth in afflicting her ; for three sons perished by sickness, and the rest closed their eyes in the sea. The tearful woman is ever seen complaining like a nightingale by the grave-stones, and upbraiding the deep like a halcyon.

poems.title: Book IX, 267
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Sailing of late on the Icarian sea, Damis, the son of Nicaretus, slipped from the deck and fell into the sea. Sore did his father pray to the immortals, and call on the water, beseeching the waves for his son. But, devoured by the sea, he perished miserably. That is a sea that of old, too, was deaf to a father’s prayers.’

poems.title: Book IX, 274
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: The young cow, obeying the goad that pricks her thighs, cuts the recurring furrows of the field, and again, after her ploughing-labour under the yoke, suffers fresh pain in suckling her newly-born calf. Do not drive her hard, husbandman. This little calf of hers, if you spare the mother, will grow up for you and become a steer.

poems.title: Book IX, 285
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: No longer does the mighty-tusked elephant, with turreted back and ready to fight phalanxes, charge unchecked into the battle; but in fear he hath yielded his thick neck to the yoke, and draws the car of divine Caesar. The wild beast knows the delight of peace; discarding the accoutrement of war, he conducts instead the father of good order.

poems.title: Book IX, 290
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: When with the blasts of the Libyan wind, the fierce Sirocco, the sea grew dark and belched up the sand from her profoundest depths, when every mast had fallen into the hollow of the deep and the lost merchant ship was drifting to Hades, Lysistratus called on the gods who help mariners, and they, for the sake of the temple ministrant alone, lulled the savage waves.

poems.title: Book IX, 293
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Xerxes, looking on the great frame of self-slain Leonidas, clothed it in a purple cloak. Then Sparta’s great hero called from the dead: “I accept not the reward due to traitors. My shield is the best ornament of my tomb. Away with the Persian frippery, and I shall go even to Hades as a Spartan.”

poems.title: Book IX, 299
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: We meek-necked oxen, the ploughers of the field, endure in the sea the labour of the land. We both draw in the water a furrow not cut by iron, the long ropes attached to the seine. We toil now for fish, not for corn. Ah, long-suffering creatures! Oxen have begun to plough the sea too for its fruits.

poems.title: Book IX, 307
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Daphne, who once refused Phoebus, now uprears her dark-leaved bough from the altar of Caesar, having found a better god than that former one. Though she hated the son of Leto, she desires Zeus the son of Aeneas. She struck root not in the Earth, her mother, but in a stone. Not even stone can refuse to bear offspring to Caesar.

poems.title: Book IX, 311
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: A sitcu, that vied in swiftness with the deer, was wounded, when heavy with young, in her generative organs. The scab of the wound in a short time entirely closed the orifice, and the pains of labour were at hand. But a man operated on her, terribly though she howled, and the dear little ones leapt forth from her womb. ‘The gracious aid of Artemis in labour is a thing of the past, and Ares, on the other hand, has begun to practise midwifery.

poems.title: Book IX, 416: On the Same
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: I am a ship built from the business of Cypris, and betake me to the sea that gave birth to that goddess ; for the man who made me was a merchant of beauty, and christened me Courtesan, for I am friendly to all. Board me confidently ; I don’t demand a heavy fare; I receive all comers. I carry both natives and foreigners ; you can row me either on land or in the sea.

poems.title: Book IX, 438
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: When the burrowing ants, the army of the earth, nibbled at the rustic bee-keeper’s sweet dainty, the old man in anger set the jar in a dish of water, thinking that, being creatures of the land, they would not get to it. But they, setting up fresh stalks of straw against it, quickly found their way, without anyone to steer them, to the vessel. So their dear belly induced even these tiny creatures to migrate from earth to water, the very newest variety of boatmen.

poems.title: Book IX, 543
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: The well-mounted troupe of bull-fighters from Thessaly, armed against the beasts with no weapons but their hands, spur their horses to run alongside the galloping bull, bent on throwing round its neck the noose of their arms. At the same time pulling it towards the ground by thus hanging themselves at the end of its neck and weighing down its head, they roll over even such a powerful brute.

poems.title: Book IX, 553: On the Foundation of Nicopolis by Augustus
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: To replace Leucas, and fertile Ambracia, and Thyrreum, and Anactorium, and Amphilochian Argos, and all the surrounding cities that the furious onslaught of war destroyed, Caesar founded me, Nicopolis, a divine city. Phoebus receives this reward for the victory of Actium.

poems.title: Book IX, 561
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: What desert, sunless hill of Northern Scythia nourished thee, wild vine? Or was it the eternal ice of the snowy Celtic Alps or the iron-bearing soil of Spain—thee, who didst bear the sour grapes, the unripened clusters—that yielded this harsh juice? I seek for thy hands, Lycurgus, to tear up by the roots the whole plant of that vine, the mother of crude fruit.

poems.title: Book IX, 575
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Heaven shall sooner quench its stars and the sun make bright the face of night; the sea shall sooner provide sweet water for mortals to draw, and the dead return to the land of the living, than oblivion of those ancient pages shall rob us of the glorious name of Homer.

poems.title: Book IX, 708
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: The barbarian bridged the Hellespont in his daring folly, but Time dissolved all that labour. Now Dicaearchia has made the sea a continent, and given the depths the form of dry land. She fixed firmly in the depths a vast supporting structure of stone, and with the hands of the Giants made the water beneath stand still. We could always sail over the sea, but insecure as it was for sailors who travelled on it, it has now promised to remain secure for foot-travellers.

poems.title: Book IX, 709: On the Bronze Statue of the Eurotas by Eutychides
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: The artist moulded Eurotas fresh from his bath of - fire, as if still wet and immersed in his stream. For all his limbs are pliant and liquid as water, and he moves flowingly from his head to the tips of his fingers and toes. Art vied with the river. Who was it that coaxed the bronze statue to riot along more liquidly than water?

poems.title: Book IX, 742
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Take off from my neck, husbandman, the collar, and free me from the iron furrow-cutter; for Myron did not make my bronze into flesh, but his art gave me the aspect of being alive, so that often I even wished to low. He did not, however, let me go to work, but tied me to a base.

poems.title: Book IX, 777
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Look how proudly the art of the worker in bronze makes this horse stand. Fierce is his glance as he arches his neck and shakes out his wind-tossed mane for the course. I believe that if a charioteer were to fit the bit to his jaws and prick him with the spur, thy work, Lysippus, would surprise us by running away; for Art makes it breathe.

poems.title: Book IX, 778: On a Tapestry
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: In me Carpo, imitating all by her shuttle’s labour at the loom, depicted accurately all the fruitful land, encompassed by Ocean, that obeys great Caesar, and the blue sea as well. I come to Caesar as a present ...., for it was the queen’s duty to offer the gift long due to the gods.

poems.title: Book XI, 33
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Secretly advancing, O ivy, thy twisted creeping foot, thou throttlest me, the vine, sweet gift of Bacchus, mother of clusters. But thou dost not so much fetter me as thou dost destroy thine own honour ; for who would set ivy on his brows without pouring out wine?

poems.title: Book XI, 36
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: When you were pretty, Archestratus, and the hearts of the young men were burnt for your wine-red cheeks, there was no talk of friendship with me, but sporting with others you spoilt your prime like a rose. Now, however, when you begin to blacken with horrid hair, you would force me to be your friend, offering me the straw after giving the harvest to others.

poems.title: Book XI, 173
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: If you have lent out some of it, and give some now, and are going to give some more, you are never master of your money.

poems.title: Book XI, 321
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Grammarians, ye children of Stygian Momus, ye book-worms feeding on thorns, demon foes of books, dogs of Zenodotus, soldiers of Callimachus from whom, though you hold him out as a shield, you do not refrain your tongue, hunters of melancholy conjunctions who take delight in mzn and sphin and in enquiring if the Cyclops had dogs, may ye wear yourselves away for all eternity, ye wretches, muttering abuse of others; then come and quench your venom in me.

poems.title: Book XI, 347
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Farewell ye whose eyes ever range over the universe, and ye thorn-gathering book-worms of Aristarchus’ school. What serves it me to enquire what path the Sun has run, and whose son was Proteus and who Pygmalion? Let me know works whose lines are clear, but let dark lore waste away the devotees of Callimachus.

poems.title: Book XIII, 1
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Hail, Paphian goddess! For all mortals, creatures of the day, ever honour by all fair words and works thy power and immortal beauty and loveable majesty; for ever and to all dost thou manifest thy dignity.

poems.title: Book XVI, 25
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: If thou hast ever heard of Demostratus from Sinope, who twice won the Isthmian pine-wreath, it is he whom thou lookest on, he whose back never left its seal on the sand from a fall in limber wrestling bouts. Gaze at his countenance animated by pluck like a savage beast’s, how it preserves its ancient look of keenness to win. And the bronze says, “Let my base set me free, and like a living man I will dight me again for the combat.”

poems.title: Book XVI, 52
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Perhaps, O stranger, seeing me thus with a belly like a bull and with solidly built limbs, like a second Atlas, thou marvellest, doubting if I am of mortal nature. But know that I am Heras of Laodicea, the all-round fighter, crowned by Smyrna and the oak of Pergamus, by Delphi, Corinth, Elis, Argos, and Actium. But if thou enquirest as to my victories in other contests thou shalt number also the sands of Libya.

poems.title: Book XVI, 81: On the Statue of Zeus at Olympia
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Either God came from Heaven to Earth to show thee His image, Phidias, or thou didst go to see God.

poems.title: Book XVI, 93: On the Same
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: I slew the vast wild beast of Nemea, I slew the hydra and the bull, and smashed the jaw of the boar; when I had torn off the girdle I took the horses of Diomede. After plucking the golden apples I captured Geryon. Augeas learnt to know me, the hind did not escape me, and I killed the birds. I led Cerberus, and myself dwell in Olympus.

poems.title: Book XVI, 104: On the Same
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: So Hera, then, wished for this to crown all his labours, the sight of doughty Heracles stripped of his arms! Where is the lion-skin cloak, where the quiver of loud-whizzing arrows on his shoulder and the heavy-footed branch, the slayer of beasts? Love has stripped thee of all, and it is not strange that, having made Zeus a swan, he deprived Heracles of his weapons.

poems.title: Book XVI, 137: On the Same
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Who, lawless Colchian, chronicled thy wrath in the picture? Who wrought thee, thus barbarous even in thy image? Dost thou yet thirst for thy babes’ blood? Is some second Jason or another Glauce, thy pretext? Out on thee, murderess of thy children, even in the painted wax. For the very picture feels that jealousy of thine that passed all bounds.

poems.title: Book XVI, 141: On the Same
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: How, twittering swallow, didst thou suffer to have as nurse of thy children the Colchian woman, the vengeful destroyer of her babes, from whose blood-shot eye still flashes murderous fire, from whose jaws white foam still drips, whose sword is freshly bathed in blood? Fly from the fatal mother, who even in the wax is still slaying her children.

poems.title: Book XVI, 177: On the Same
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Laughter-loving Aphrodite, minister of the bridal chamber, who girt thee, honey-sweet goddess that thou art, with the weapons of war? To thee the Paean is dear, and golden-haired Hymenaeus and the dulcet charm of shrill-voiced flutes. Why hast thou put on these engines of murder? Is it that thou hast despoiled bold Ares to boast how great is the might of Cypris?

poems.title: Book XVI, 193
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: A. May I touch the kail, Cyllenian? B. No, traveller. A. Why grudge some greens? B. It is not grudging, but it is the law to keep pilfering hands from other people’s property. A. Well! that is strange. Hermes has made a new law against stealing.

poems.title: Book XVI, 215: On the Same
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: Look how the Loves, having plundered Olympus, deck themselves in the arms of the immortals, exulting in their spoils. They bear the bow of Phoebus, the thunderbolt of Zeus, the shield and helmet of Ares, the club of Heracles, the three-pronged spear of the sea-god, the thyrse of Bacchus, Hermes’ winged sandals, and Artemis’ torches. Mortals need not grieve that they must yield to the arrows of the Loves, if the gods have given them their arms wherewith to busk themselves.

poems.title: Book XVI, 240: On the Same
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text: A (a traveller). I see the figs are ripe. Won’t you let me take a few? B (Priapus). Don’t touch a single one. A. How angry Priapus is! B. You will say so still, and you will have come to no purpose. A. Indeed, I beseech you. B. Give me; for I, too, am in want of something. A. What do you want anything from me? B. There is a law, I think, “Give and take.” A. Even though you are a god, are you greedy for money? B. It is another thing that I am fond of. A. What is that? B. If you eat my figs, give me with a good grace that fig you have behind.

poems.title: To Apollo of Leucas (Mackail)
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Phoebus who holdest the sheer steep of Leucas, far seen of mariners and washed by the Ionian sea, receive of sailors this mess of hand-kneaded barley bread and a libation mingled in a little cup, and the gleam of a brief-shining lamp that drinks with half-saturate mouth from a sparing oil-flask; in recompence whereof be gracious, and send on their sails a favourable wind to run with them to the harbours of Actium.

poems.title: To Artemis the Healer (Mackail)
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Huntress and archer, maiden daughter of Zeus and Leto, Artemis to whom are given the recesses of the mountains, this very day send away beyond the North Wind this hateful sickness from the best of kings; for so above thine altars will Philippus offer vapour of frankincense, doing goodly sacrifice of a hill-pasturing boar.

poems.title: To the Corn Goddess (Mackail)
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Those handfuls of corn from the furrows of a tiny field, Demeter lover of wheat, Sosicles the tiller dedicates to thee, having reaped now an abundant harvest; but again likewise may he carry back his sickle blunted from shearing of the straw.

poems.title: Fate's Persistency (Mackail)
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: I Philaenion who gave birth but for the pyre, I the woeful mother, I who had seen the threefold grave of my children, anchored my trust on another's pangs; for I surely hoped that he at least would live, whom I had not borne. So I, who once had fair children, brought up an adopted son; but God would not let me have even a second mother's grace; for being called ours he perished, and now I am become a woe to the rest of mothers too.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IV.2: ἄνθεά σοι δρέψας Ἑλικώνια,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ἄνθεά σοι δρέψας Ἑλικώνια, καὶ κλυτοδένδρου
Πιερίης κείρας πρωτοφύτους κάλυκας,
καὶ σελίδος νεαρῆς θερίσας στάχυν, ἀντανέπλεξα
τοῖς Μελεαγρείοις ὡς ἴκελον στεφάνοις.
ἀλλὰ παλαιοτέρων εἰδὼς κλέος, ἐσθλὲ Κάμιλλε,
γνῶθι καὶ ὁπλοτέρων τὴν ὀλιγοστιχίην.
Ἀντίπατρος πρέψει στεφάνῳ στάχυς· ὡς δὲ κόρυμβος
Κριναγόρας λάμψει δʼ ὡς βότρυς Ἀντίφιλος,
Τύλλιος ὡς μελίλωτον, ἀμάρακον ὣς Φιλόδημος·
μύρτα δʼ ὁ Παρμενίων· ὡς ῥόδον Ἀντιφάνης·
κισσὸς δʼ Αὐτομέδων Ζωνᾶς κρίνα δρῦς δὲ Βιάνωρ·
Ἀντίγονος δʼ ἐλάη, καὶ Διόδωρος ἴον
Εὔηνον δάφνῃ, συνεπιπλεκτοὺς δὲ περισσοὺς
εἴκασον οἷς ἐθέλεις ἄνθεσιν ἀρτιφύτοις.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.5: Δούνακας ἀκροδέτους, καὶ τὴν
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Δούνακας ἀκροδέτους, καὶ τὴν ἁλινηχέα κώπην,
γυρῶν τʼ ἀγκίστρων λαιμοδακεῖς ἀκίδας,
καὶ λίνον ἀκρομόλιβδον, ἀπαγγελτῆρά τε κύρτου
φελλόν, καὶ δισσὰς σχοινοπλεκεῖς σπυρίδας,
καὶ τὸν ἐγερσιφαῆ πυρὸς ἔγκυον ἔμφλογα πέτρον,
ἄγκυράν τε, νεῶν πλαζομένων παγίδα.
Πείσων ὁ γριπεὺς Ἑρμῇ πόρεν, ἔντρομος ἤδη
δεξιτερήν, πολλοῖς βριθόμενος καμάτοις.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.36: δράγματά σοι χώρου μικραύλακος,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
δράγματά σοι χώρου μικραύλακος, ὦ φιλόπυρε
Δηοῖ, Σωσικλέης θῆκεν ἀρουροπόνος,
εὔσταχυν ἀμήσας τὸν νῦν σπόρον· ἀλλὰ καὶ αὖτις ,
ἐκ καλαμητομίης ἀμβλὺ φέροι δρέπανον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.38: δίκτυά σοι μολίβῳ στεφανούμενα,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
δίκτυά σοι μολίβῳ στεφανούμενα, δυσιθάλασσα,
καὶ κώπην, ἅλμης τὴν μεθύουσαν ἔτι,
κητοφόνον τε τρίαιναν, ἐν ὕδασι καρτερὸν ἔγχος,
καὶ τὸν ἀεὶ φελλοῖς κύρτον ἐλεγχόμενον,
ἄγκυράν τε, νεῶν στιβαρὴν χέρα, καὶ φιλοναύτην
σπέρμα πυρὸς σῴζειν πέτρον ἐπιστάμενον,
ἀρχιθάλασσε Πόσειδον, Ἀμύντιχος ὕστατα δῶρα
θήκατʼ, ἐπεὶ μογερῆς παύσαθʼ ἁλιπλανίης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.62: κυκλοτερῆ μόλιβον. σελίδων σημάντορα
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
κυκλοτερῆ μόλιβον. σελίδων σημάντορα πλευρῆς,
καὶ σμίλαν, δονάκων ἀκροβελῶν γλυφίδα,
καὶ κανονῖδʼ ὑπάτην, καὶ τὴν παρὰ θῖνα κίσηριν,
αὐχμηρὸν πόντου τρηματόεντα λίθον,
Καλλιμένης Μούσαις, ἀποπαυσάμενος καμάτοιο,
θῆκεν ἐπεὶ γήρᾳ κανθὸς ἐπεσκέπετο.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.90: ἄγκυραν ἐμβρύοικον, ἐρυσινηίδα,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ἄγκυραν ἐμβρύοικον, ἐρυσινηίδα,
κώπας τε δισσὰς τὰς ἀπωσικυμάτους,
καὶ δικτύοις μόλιβδον ἡψιδωμένον,
κύρτους τε φελλοῖς τοὺς ἐπεσφραγισμένους,
καὶ πῖλον ἀμφίκρηνον ὑδασιστεγῆ,
λίθον τε ναύταις ἑσπέρης πυρσητόκον,
ἁλὸς τύραννε, σοί, Πόσειδον, Ἀρχικλῆς
ἔθηκε, λήξας τῆς ἐπʼ ᾐόνων ἄλης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.92: αὐλὸν καμινευτῆρα τὸν φιλήνεμον,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
αὐλὸν καμινευτῆρα τὸν φιλήνεμον,
ῥίνην τε κνησίχρυσον ὀξυδήκτορα,
καὶ τὸν δίχηλον καρκίνον πυραγρέτην,
πτωκὸς πόδας τε τούσδε λειψανηλόγους,
ὁ χρυσοτέκτων Δημοφῶν Κυλληνίῳ
ἔθηκε, γήρᾳ κανθὸν ἐζοφωμένος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.94: Ἀραξόχειρα ταῦτά σοι τὰ
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Ἀραξόχειρα ταῦτά σοι τὰ τύμπανα,
καὶ κύμβαλʼ ὀξύδουπα κοιλοχείλεα,
διδύμους τε λωτοὺς κεροβόας, ἐφʼ οἷς ποτε
ἐπωλόλυξεν αὐχένα στροβιλίσας,
λυσιφλεβῆ τε σάγαριν ἀμφιθηγέα,
λεοντόδιφρε, σοί, Ῥέη, Κλυτοσθένης
ἔθηκε, λυσσητῆρα γηράσας πόδα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.99: κόψας ἐκ φηγοῦ σε
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
κόψας ἐκ φηγοῦ σε τὸν αὐτόφλοιον ἔθηκεν
Πᾶνα Φιλοξενίδης, ὁ κλυτὸς αἰγελάτης,
θύσας αἰγιβάτην πολιὸν τράγον, ἔν τε γάλακτι
πρωτογόνῳ βωμοὺς τοὺς ἱεροὺς μεθύσας.
ἀνθʼ ὧν ἐν σηκοῖς διδυμητόκοι αἶγες ἔσονται
γαστέρα, φεύγουσαι τρηχὺν ὀδόντα λύκου,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.101: ξίφη τὰ πολλῶν κνωδάλων
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ξίφη τὰ πολλῶν κνωδάλων λαιμητόμα
πυριτρόφους τε ῥιπίδας πορηνέμους,
ἠθμόν τε πουλύτρητον, ἠδὲ τετράπουν
πυρὸς γέφυραν, ἐσχάρην κρεηδόκον,
ζωμήρυσίν τε τὴν λίπους ἀφρηλόγον,
ὁμοῦ κρεάγρῃ τῇ σιδηροδακτύλῳ,
βραδυσκελὴς Ἥφαιστε, σοὶ Τιμασίων
ἔθηκεν, ἀκμῆς γυῖον ὠρφανωμένος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.102: Ῥοιὴν ξανθοχίτωνα, γεραιόφλοιά τε
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Ῥοιὴν ξανθοχίτωνα, γεραιόφλοιά τε σῦκα,
καὶ ῥοδέας σταφυλῆς ὠμὸν ἀποσπάδιον,
μῆλὸν θʼ ἡδύπνουν λεπτῇ πεποκωμένον ἄχνῃ,
καὶ κάρυον χλωρῶν ἐκφανὲς ἐκ λεπίδων,
καὶ σίκυον χνοάοντα, τὸν ἐν φύλλοις πεδοκοίτην,
καὶ πέρκην ἤδη χρυσοχίτωνʼ ἐλάην,
σοί, φιλοδῖτα Πρίηπε, φυτοσκάφος ἄνθετο Λάμων,
δένδρεσι καὶ γυίοις εὐξάμενος θαλέθειν,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.103: στάθμην ἰθυτενῆ μολιβαχθέα, δουριτυπῆ
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
στάθμην ἰθυτενῆ μολιβαχθέα, δουριτυπῆ
σφῦραν, καὶ γυρὰς ἀμφιδέτους ἀρίδας,
καὶ στιβαρὸν πέλεκυν στελεχητόμον, ἰθύδρομόν τε
πρίονα, μιλτείῳ στάγματι πειθόμενον,
τρύπανά θʼ ἑλκεσίχειρα, τέρετρά τε, μιλτοφυρῆ ρε
σχοῖνον, ὑπʼ ἀκρονύχῳ ψαλλομένην κανόνι, .
σοί, κούρη γλαυκῶπι, Λεόντιχος ὤπασε δῶρον,
ἄνθος ἐπεὶ γυίων πᾶν ἀπέδυσε χρόνος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.104: Σπερμοφόρον πήρην ὠμαχθέα, κὠλεσίβωλον
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Σπερμοφόρον πήρην ὠμαχθέα, κὠλεσίβωλον
σφῦραν, καὶ γαμψὰς πυρολόγους δρεπάνας,
καὶ τριβόλους ὀξεῖς ἀχυρότριβας, ἱστοβόην τε
σὺν γυροῖς ἀρότροις, καὶ φιλόγαιον ὕνιν,
κέντρα τʼ ὀπισθονυγῆ, καὶ βουστρόφα δεσμὰ τενόντων,
καὶ τρίνακας ξυλίνας, χεῖρας ἀρουροπονων,
γυῖʼ ἅτε πηρωθεὶς Λυσίξενος αὔλακι πολλῇ
ἐκρέμασεν Δηοῖ τῇ σταχυοστεφάνῳ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.107: Ὑλησκόπῳ με Πανὶ θηρευτὴς
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Ὑλησκόπῳ με Πανὶ θηρευτὴς Γέλων
ἔθηκε λόγχην, ἧς ἀπέθρισε χρόνος
ἀκμὴν ἐν ἔργῳ, καὶ λίνων πολυστρόφων
γεραιὰ τρύχη, καὶ πάγας δεραγχέας,
νευροπλεκεῖς τε κνωδάλων ἐπισφύρους
ὠκεῖς ποδίστρας, καὶ τραχηλοδεσπότας
κλοιοὺς κυνούχους· γυῖα γὰρ δαμεὶς χρόνῳ
ἀπεῖπεν ἤδη τὴν ὀρεινόμον πλάνην.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.231: Αἰγύπτου μεδέουσα μελαμβώλου, λινόπεπλε
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Αἰγύπτου μεδέουσα μελαμβώλου, λινόπεπλε
δαῖμον, ἐπʼ εὐϊέρους βῆθι θυηπολίας.
σοὶ γὰρ ὑπὲρ σχιδάκων λαγαρὸν ποπάνευμα πρόκειται,
καὶ πολιὸν χηνῶν ζεῦγος ἐνυδροβίων,
καὶ νάρδος ψαφαρὴ κεγχρίτισιν ἰσχάσιν ἀμφί,
καὶ σταφυλὴ γραίη, χὠ μελίπνους λίβανος.
εἰ δʼ ὡς ἐκ πελάγους ἐρρύσαο Δᾶμιν, ἄνασσα,
κἠκ πενίης, θύσει χρυσόκερων κεμάδα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.236: ἔμβολα χαλκογένεια, φιλόπλοα τεύχεα
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ἔμβολα χαλκογένεια, φιλόπλοα τεύχεα νηῶν,
Ἀκτιακοῦ πολέμου κείμενα μαρτύρια,
ἠνίδε σιμβλεύει κηρότροφα δῶρα μελισσῶν,
ἑσμῷ βομβητῇ κυκλόσε βριθόμενα.
Καίσαρος εὐνομίης χρηστὴ χάρις· ὅπλα γὰρ ἐχθρῶν
καρποὺς εἰρήνης ἀντεδίδαξε τρέφειν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.240: Ζηνὸς καὶ Λητοῦς θηροσκόπε
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Ζηνὸς καὶ Λητοῦς θηροσκόπε τοξότι κούρη,
Ἄρτεμις, ἣ θαλάμους τοὺς ὀρέων ἔλαχες,
νοῦσον τὴν στυγερὴν αὐθημερὸν ἐκ βασιλῆος
ἐσθλοτάτου πέμψαις ἄχρις Ὑπερβορέων·
σοὶ γὰρ ὑπὲρ βωμῶν ἀτμὸν λιβάνοιο Φίλιππος
ῥέξει, καλλιθυτῶν κάπρον ὀρειονόμον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.247: κερκίδας ὀρθρολάλοισι χελιδόσιν εἰκελοφώνους,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
κερκίδας ὀρθρολάλοισι χελιδόσιν εἰκελοφώνους,
Παλλάδος ἱστοπόνου λειομίτους κάμακας,
καὶ κτένα κοσμοκόμην, καὶ δακτυλότριπτον ἄτρακτον
σφονδυλοδινήτῳ νήματι νηχόμενον,
καὶ τάλαρον σχοίνοις ὑφασμένον, ὃν ποτʼ ὀδόντι
ἐπλήρου τολύπη πᾶσα καθαιρομένη,
σοί, φιλέριθε κόρη Παλλαντιάς, ἡ βαθύγηρως
Αἰσιόνη, πενίης δῶρον, ἀνεκρέμασεν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.251: Λευκάδος· αἰπὺν ἔχων ναύταις
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Λευκάδος· αἰπὺν ἔχων ναύταις τηλέσκοπον ὄχθον,
Φοῖβε, τὸν Ἰονίῳ λουόμενον πελάγει,
δέξαι πλωτήρων μάζης χεριφυρέα δαῖτα,
καὶ σπονδὴν ὀλίγῃ κιρναμένην κύλικι,
καὶ βραχυφεγγίτου λύχνου σέλας ἐκ βιοφειδοῦς
ὄλπης ἡμιμεθεῖ πινόμενον στόματι·
ἀνθʼ ὧν ἱλήκοις, ἐπὶ δʼ ἱστία πέμψον ἀήτην
οὔριον Ἀκτιακοὺς σύνδρομον εἰς λιμένας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.259: τίς τὸν ἄχνουν Ἑρμῆν
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
τίς τὸν ἄχνουν Ἑρμῆν σε παρʼ ὑσπλήγεσσιν ἔθηκεν;— Ἑρμογένης. — τίνος ὤν; — Δαϊμένευς. — ποδαπός; —
Ἀντιοχεύς. — τιμῶν σε χάριν τίνος;— “ὡς συναρωγὸν
ἐν σταδίοις.”— ποίοις;— Ἰσθμόθι κἠν Νεμέᾳ. —
ἔτρεχε γάρ; — καὶ πρῶτος. — ἑλὼν τίνας; — “Ἐννέ παῖδας·
ἔπτη δʼ ὡς ἂν ἔχων τοὺς πόδας ἡμετέρους.”

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.186: ἄρτι μὲν ἐν θαλάμοις
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ἄρτι μὲν ἐν θαλάμοις Νικιππίδος ἡδὺς ἐπήχει
λωτός, καὶ γαμικοῖς † ὕμνος ἔχαιρε κρότοις·
θρῆνος δʼ εἰς ὑμέναιον ἐκώμασεν ἡ δὲ τάλαινα,
οὔπω πάντα γυνή, καὶ νέκυς ἐβλέπετο.
δακρυόεις Ἀίδη, τί πόσιν νύμφης διέλυσας,
αὐτὸς ἐφʼ ἁρπαγίμοις τερπόμενος λέχεσιν;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.187: ἡ γρῆυς Νικὼ Μελίτης
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ἡ γρῆυς Νικὼ Μελίτης τάφον ἐστεφάνωσε
παρθενικῆς. Ἀίδη, τοῦθʼ ὁσίως κέκρικας;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.234: Αἴλιος ὁ θρασύχειρ Ἄρεος
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Αἴλιος ὁ θρασύχειρ Ἄρεος πρόμος, ὁ ψελιώσας
αὐχένα χρυσοδέτοις ἐκ πολέμου στεφάνοις,
τηξιμελεῖ νούσῳ κεκολουμένος, ἔδραμε θυμῷ
ἐς προτέρην ἔργων ἄρσενα μαρτυρίην,
ὦσε δʼ ὑπὸ σπλάγχνοις πλατὺ φάσγανον, ἓν μόνον εἰπών
ἄνδρας Ἄρης κτείνει, δειλοτέρους δὲ νόσος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.362: ἐνθάδε τὴν ἱερὴν κεφαλὴν
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ἐνθάδε τὴν ἱερὴν κεφαλὴν σορὸς ἥδε κέκευθεν
Ἀετίου χρηστοῦ, ῥήτορος ἐκπρεπέος.
ἦλθεν δʼ
εἰς Ἀίδαο δέμας, ψυχὴ δʼ ἐν Ὀλύμπῳ
τέρπεθʼ ἅμα Ζηνὶ καὶ ἄλλοισιν μακάρεσσι
ἀθάνατον δὲ
οὔτε λόγος ποιεῖν οὔτε θεὸς δύναται.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.382: ἠπείρῳ μʼ ἀποδοῦσα νέκυν,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ἠπείρῳ μʼ ἀποδοῦσα νέκυν, τρηχεῖα θάλασσα,
σύρεις καὶ τέφρης λοιπὸν ἔτι σκύβαλον.
κἠν Ἀίδῃ ναυηγὸς ἐγὼ μόνος, οὐδʼ ἐπὶ χέρσου
εἰρήνην ἕξω φρικαλέης σπιλάδος.
ἢ τύμβευέ κενοῦσα καθʼ ὕδατος, ἢ παραδοῦσα
γαίῃ, τὸν κείνης μηκέτι κλέπτε νέκυν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.383: ᾘόνιον τόδε σῶμα βροτοῦ
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ᾘόνιον τόδε σῶμα βροτοῦ παντλήμονος ἄθρει
σπαρτόν, ἁλιρραγέων ἐκχύμενον σκοπέλων
τῇ μὲν ἐρημοκόμης κεῖται καὶ χῆρος ὀδόντων
κόρση· τῇ δὲ χερῶν πενταφυεῖς ὄνυχες,
πλευρά τε σαρκολιπῆ, ταρσοὶ δʼ ἑτέρωθεν ἄμοιροι
νεύρων, καὶ κώλων ἔκλυτος ἁρμονίη.
οὗτος ὁ πουλυμερὴς εἷς ἦν ποτε. φεῦ μακαριστοί,
ὅσσοι ἀπʼ ὠδίνων οὐκ ἴδον ἠέλιον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.385: ἥρως Πρωτεσίλαε, σὺ γὰρ
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ἥρως Πρωτεσίλαε, σὺ γὰρ πρώτην ἐμύησας
Ἴλιον Ἑλλαδικοῦ θυμὸν ἰδεῖν δόρατος,
καὶ περὶ σοῖς τύμβοις ὅσα δένδρεα μακρὰ τέθηλε,
πάντα τὸν εἰς Τροίην ἐγκεκύηκε χόλον
Ἴλιον ἢν ἐσίδῃ γὰρ ἀπʼ ἀκρεμόνων κορυφαίων,
καρφοῦται, πετάλων κόσμον ἀναινόμενα.
θυμὸν ἐπὶ Τροίῃ πόσον ἔζεσας, ἡνίκα τὴν σὴν
σῴζει καὶ στελέχη μῆνιν ἐπʼ ἀντιπάλους.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.394: Μυλεργάτας ἀνήρ με κἠν
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Μυλεργάτας ἀνήρ με κἠν ζωᾶς χρόνοις
βαρυβρομήταν εἶχε δινητὸν πέτρον,
πυρηφάτον Δάματρος εὐκάρπου λάτριν,
καὶ κατθανὼν στάλωσε τῷδʼ ἐπʼ ἠρίῳ,
σύνθημα τέχνας· ὣς ἔχει μʼ ἀεὶ βαρύν,
καὶ ζῶν ἐν ἔργοις, καὶ θανὼν ἐπʼ ὀστέοις.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.405: ξεῖνε, φεῦγε τὸν χαλαζεπῆ
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ξεῖνε, φεῦγε τὸν χαλαζεπῆ τάφον
τὸν φρικτὸν Ἱππώνακτος, οὗτε χἀ τέφρα
ἰαμβιάζει Βουπάλειον ἐς στύγος,
μή πως ἐγείρῃς σφῆκα τὸν κοιμώμενον,
ὃς οὐδʼ ἐν ᾅδῃ νῦν κεκοίμικεν χόλον,
σκάζουσι μέτροις ὀρθὰ τοξεύσας ἔπη

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.554: Λατύπος Ἀρχιτέλης Ἀγαθάνορι παιδὶ
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Λατύπος Ἀρχιτέλης Ἀγαθάνορι παιδὶ θανόντι
χερσὶν ὀιζυραῖς ἡρμολόγησε τάφον,
αἰαῖ, πέτρον ἐκεῖνον, ὃν οὐκ ἐκόλαψε σίδηρος,
ἀλλʼ ἐτάκη πυκινοῖς δάκρυσι τεγγόμενος.
φεῦ, στήλη φθιμένῳ κούφη μένε, κεῖνος ἵνʼ εἴπῃ·
ὄντως πατρῴη χεὶρ ἐπέθηκε λίθον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.22: νηδύι βριθομένην δάμαλιν Λητωίδι
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
νηδύι βριθομένην δάμαλιν Λητωίδι κούρῃ]
στῆσαν νηοκόροι θῦμα χαριζόμενοι, .
ἧς ἀίδην μέλλοντα προέφθασεν εὔστοχος ὠδίς,
πέμφθη δʼ εἰς ἀγέλην τεκνογονεῖν ἄφετος.
ἡ θεὸς ὠδίνων γὰρ ἐπίσκοπος οὐδʼ ἐδίκαζεν
τικτούσας κτείνειν, ἃς ἐλεεῖν ἔμαθεν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.56: Ἕβρου Θρηικίου κρυμῷ πεπεδημένον
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Ἕβρου Θρηικίου κρυμῷ πεπεδημένον ὕδωρ
νήπιος εἰσβαίνων οὐκ ἔφυγεν θάνατον
ἐς ποταμὸν δʼ ἤδη λαγαρούμενον ἴχνος ὀλισθὼν,
κρυμῷ τοὺς ἁπαλοὺς αὐχένας ἀμφεκάρη.
καὶ τὸ μὲν ἐξεσύρη λοιπὸν δέμας· ἡ δὲ μένουσα
ὄψις ἀναγκαίην εἶχε τάφου πρόφασιν.
δύσμορος ἧς ὠδῖνα διείλατο πῦρ τε καὶ ὕδωρ·
ἀμφοτέρων δὲ δοκῶν, οὐδενός ἐστιν ὅλως.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.83: νηὸς ἐπειγομένης ὠκὺν δρόμον
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
νηὸς ἐπειγομένης ὠκὺν δρόμον ἀμφεχόρευον
δελφῖνες, πελάγους ἰχθυφάγοι σκύλακες.
καπροφόνος δὲ κύων θηρσὶν κείνους ἰκελώσας
δύσμορος, ὡς ἐπὶ γῆν εἰς βυθὸν ἐξέθορεν.
ὤλετο δʼ ἀλλοτρίης θήρης χάριν· οὐ γὰρ ἐλαφρὸς
πάντων ἐστὶ κυνῶν ὁ δρόμος ἐν πελάγει.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.85: νῆα μὲν ὤλεσε πόντος,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
νῆα μὲν ὤλεσε πόντος, ἐμοὶ δʼ ἔπορεν πάλι δαίμων
πλαζομένῳ φύσεως νῆα ποθεινοτέρην·
πατρὸς ἰδὼν γὰρ ἐγὼ δέμας εἰς ἐμὲ καίριον ἐλθόν,
μουνερέτης ἐπέβην, φόρτος ὀφειλόμενος.
ἤγαγεν εἰς λιμένας δὲ καὶ ἔσπειρεν δὶς ὁ πρέσβυς,
νήπιον ἐν γαίῃ, δεύτερον ἐν πελάγει.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.88: μεμφομένη Βορέην ἐπεπωτώμην ὑπὲρ
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
μεμφομένη Βορέην ἐπεπωτώμην ὑπὲρ ἅλμης·
πνεῖ γὰρ ἐμοὶ Θρῄκης ἤπιος οὐδʼ ἄνεμος.
ἀλλά με τὴν μελίγηρυν ἀηδόνα δέξατο νώτοις
δελφίν, καὶ πτηνὴν πόντιος ἡνιόχει.
πιστοτάτῳ δʼ ἐρέτῃ πορθμευομένη, τὸν ἄκωπον
ναύτην τῇ στομάτων θέλγον ἐγὼ κιθάρῃ.
εἰρεσίην δελφῖνες ἀεὶ Μούσῃσιν ἄμισθον
ἤνυσαν οὐ ψεύστης μῦθος Ἀριόνιος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.89: λιμὸν ὀιζυρὴν ἀπαμυνομένη πολύγηρως
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
λιμὸν ὀιζυρὴν ἀπαμυνομένη πολύγηρως
Νικὼ σὺν κούραις ἠκρολόγει στάχυας·
ὤλετο δʼ ἐκ θάλπους· τῇ δʼ ἐκ καλάμης συνέριθοι
νῆσαν πυρκαϊὴν ἄξυλον ἀσταχύων.
μὴ νεμέσα, Δήμητερ, ἀπὸ χθονὸς εἰ βροτὸν οὖσαν
κοῦραι τοῖς γαίης σπέρμασιν ἠμφίεσαν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.232: Ἀδριακοῖο κύτους λαιμὸς τὸ
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Ἀδριακοῖο κύτους λαιμὸς τὸ πάλαι μελίγηρυς,
ἡνίκʼ ἐγαστροφόρουν Βακχιακὰς χάριτας,
νῦν κλασθεὶς κεῖμαι νεοθηλέι καρτερὸν ἕρκος
κλήματι, πρὸς τρυφερὴν τεινομένῳ καλύβην.
αἰεί τοι Βρομίῳ λατρεύομεν· ἢ γεραὸν γὰρ
φρουροῦμεν πιστῶς, ἢ νέον ἐκτρέφομεν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.240: βαιὸν ἀποπλανίην λιπομήτορα παῖδα
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
βαιὸν ἀποπλανίην λιπομήτορα παῖδα Καλύπτρης
κριὸς ἑλιξόκερως θεῖνε θρασυνόμενος.
κάπρος δʼ Ἡράκλειος ἀπορρήξας ἀπὸ δεσμῶν,
ἐς νηδὺν κριοῦ πᾶσαν ἔβαψε γένυν
ζωὴν νηπιάχῳ δʼ ἐχαρίσσατο. ἆρʼ † ἀπὸ Ἥρης
Ἡρακλέης βρεφέων ᾤκτισεν ἡλικίην;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.247: Εὐθηλῆ πλάτανόν με Νότου
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Εὐθηλῆ πλάτανόν με Νότου βαρυλαίλαπες αὖραι
ῥίζης ἐξ αὐτῆς ἐστόρεσαν δαπέδοις·
λουσαμένη Βρομίῳ δʼ ἔστην πάλιν, ὄμβρον ἔχουσα
χείματι καὶ θάλπει τοῦ Διὸς ἡδύτερον.
ὀλλυμένη δʼ ἔζησα· μόνη δὲ πιοῦσα Λυαῖον,
ἄλλων κλινομένων, ὀρθοτέρη βλέπομαι.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.253: ἐν Θήβαις Κάδμου κλεινὸς
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ἐν Θήβαις Κάδμου κλεινὸς γάμος, ἀλλὰ μυσαχθὴς
Οἰδίποδος· τελετὰς Εὔιος ἠσπάσατο,
ἃς γελάσας Πενθεὺς ὠδύρατο τείχεα χορδαῖς
ἔστη, καὶ λωτοῖς ἔστενε λυόμενα·
Ἀντιόπης ὁσίη, χαλεπὴ δʼ ὠδὶς Ἰοκάστης·
ἦν Ἰνὼ φιλόπαις, ἀλλʼ ἀσεβὴς Ἀθάμας.
† οἰκτρὸν ἀεὶ πτολίεθρον ἴδʼ ὡς ἐσθλῶν περὶ Θήβας
μύθων καὶ στυγνῶν ἤρκεσεν ἱστορίη.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.254: ἡ πυρὶ πάντα τεκοῦσα
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ἡ πυρὶ πάντα τεκοῦσα Φιλαίνιον, ἡ βαρυπενθὴς
μήτηρ, ἡ τέκνων τρισσὸν ἰδοῦσα τάφον,
ἀλλοτρίαις ὠδῖσιν ἐφώρμισα· ἦ γὰρ ἐώλπειν
πάντως μοι ζήσειν τοῦτον ὃν οὐκ ἔτεκον.
ἡ δʼ εὔπαις θετὸν υἱὸν ἀνήγαγον ἀλλά με δαίμων
ἤθελε μηδʼ ἄλλης μητρὸς ἔχειν χάριτα.
κληθεὶς ἡμέτερος γὰρ ἀπέφθιτο· νῦν δὲ τεκούσαις
ἤδη καὶ λοιπαῖς πένθος ἐγὼ γέγονα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.255: ἠρίθμει πολὺν ὄλβον Ἀριστείδης
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ἠρίθμει πολὺν ὄλβον Ἀριστείδης ὁ πενιχρὸς
τὴν ὄιν ὡς ποίμνην, τὴν βόα δʼ ὡς ἀγέλην
ἤμβροτε δʼ ἀμφοτέρων· ἀμνὴν λύκος, ἔκτανε δʼ ὠδὶς
τὴν δάμαλιν, πενίης δʼ ὤλετο βουκόλιον·
πηροδέτῳ δʼ ὃ γʼ ἱμάντι κατʼ αὐχένος ἅμμα πεδήσας
οἰκτρὸς ἀμυκήτῳ κάτθανε πὰρ καλύβῃ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.262: ἠρίθμουν ποτὲ πάντες Ἀριστοδίκην
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ἠρίθμουν ποτὲ πάντες Ἀριστοδίκην κλυτόπαιδα
ἑξάκις ὠδίνων ἄχθος ἀπωσαμένην
ἤρισε δʼ εἰς αὐτὴν ὕδωρ χθονί· τρεῖς γὰρ ὄλοντο
νούσῳ, λειπόμενοι δʼ ἤμυσαν ἐν πελάγει.
αἰεὶ δʼ ἡ βαρύδακρυς, ἐπὶ στήλαις μὲν ἀηδών,
μεμφομένη δὲ βυθοῖς ἀλκυονὶς βλέπεται.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.267: Ἰκαρίην πλώων [ πρῴην]
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Ἰκαρίην πλώων [ πρῴην] ἅλα, νηὸς ὀλισθὼν
Δᾶμις ὁ Νικαρέτου κάππεσεν εἰς πέλαγος.
πολλὰ πατὴρ δʼ ἠρᾶτο πρὸς ἀθανάτους, καὶ ἐς ὕδωρ
φθέγγεθʼ, ὑπὲρ τέκνου κύματα λισσόμενος.
ὤλετο δʼ οἰκτίστως βρυχθεὶς ἁλί· κεῖνο δὲ πατρὸς
ἔκλυεν ἀράων οὐδὲ πάλαι πέλαγος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.274: καὶ τὸν; ἀρουραῖον γυρήτομον
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
καὶ τὸν; ἀρουραῖον γυρήτομον αὔλακα τέμνει
μηροτυπεῖ κέντρῳ πειθομένη δάμαλις·
καὶ μετʼ ἀροτροπόνους ζεύγλας πάλι τῷ νεοθηλεῖ
πινομένη μόσχῳ δεύτερον ἄλγος ἔχει.
μὴ θλίψῃς αὐτὴν ὁ γεωμόρος· οὗτος ὁ βαιὸς
μόσχος, ἐὰν φείσῃ, σοὶ τρέφεται δαμάλης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.285: οὐκέτι πυργωθεὶς ὁ φαλαγγομάχας
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
οὐκέτι πυργωθεὶς ὁ φαλαγγομάχας ἐπὶ δῆριν
ἄσχετος ὁρμαίνει μυριόδους ἐλέφας,
ἀλλὰ φόβῳ στείλας βαθὺν αὐχένα πρὸς ζυγοδέσμους,
ἄντυγα διφρουλκεῖ Καίσαρος οὐρανίου.
ἔγνω δʼ εἰρήνης καὶ θὴρ χάριν ὄργανα ῥίψας
Ἄρεος, εὐνομίης ἀντανάγει πατέρα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.290: ὅτʼ ἐξ ἀήτου Λίβυος,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ὅτʼ ἐξ ἀήτου Λίβυος, ἐκ ζαοῦς Νότου;
συνεζοφώθη πόντος, ἐκ δὲ νειάτων
μυχῶν βυθῖτις ψάμμος ἐξηρεύγετο,
ἱστὸς δὲ πᾶς ὤλισθεν εἰς ἁλὸς πτύχας,
φορτὶς δʼ ἐσύρετʼ ἐς ἀίδαν πλανωμένη,
ἀρωγοναύτας δαίμονας Λυσίστρατος
ἐλιπάρησεν οἱ δὲ τῷ νεωκόρῳ
μούνῳ θάλασσαν ἀγρίαν ἐκοίμισαν,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.293: πουλὺ Λεωνίδεω κατιδὼν δέμας
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
πουλὺ Λεωνίδεω κατιδὼν δέμας αὐτοδάικτον
Ξέρξης ἐχλαίνου φάρεϊ πορφυρέῳ·
κἠκ νεκύων δʼ ἤχησεν ὁ τᾶς Σπάρτας πολὺς ἥρως·
“οὐ δέχομαι προδόταις μισθὸν ὀφειλόμενον
ἀσπὶς ἐμοὶ τύμβου κόσμος μέγας· αἶρε τὰ Περσῶν
χἤξω κεἰς ἀΐδην ὡς Λακεδαιμόνιοσ”

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.299: ταῦροι πρηϋτένοντες, ἀροτρευτῆρες ἀρούρης,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ταῦροι πρηϋτένοντες, ἀροτρευτῆρες ἀρούρης,
εἰν ἁλὶ τοὺς γαίης ἀντέχομεν καμάτους·
αὔλακα τὴν ἀσίδαρον ἐν ὕδασιν ἕλκομεν ἄμφω,
μακροτόνων σχοίνων ἅμμα σαγηνόδετον
ἰχθύσι δʼ ἐκ σταχύων λατρεύομεν. ἆ ταλαεργοί·
ἤδη κἠν πελάγει καρπὸν ἀροῦσι βόες.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.307: Φοῖβον ἀνηναμένη Δάφνη ποτέ,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Φοῖβον ἀνηναμένη Δάφνη ποτέ, νῦν ἀνέτειλεν
Καίσαρος ἐκ βωμοῦ κλῶνα μελαμπέταλον
ἐκ δὲ θεοῦ θεὸν εὗρεν ἀμείνονα· Λητοΐδην γὰρ
ἐχθήρασα, θέλει Ζῆνα τὸν Αἰνεάδην.
ῥίζαν δʼ οὐκ ἀπὸ γῆς μητρὸς βάλεν, ἀλλʼ ἀπὸ πέτρης.
Καίσαρι μὴ τίκτειν οὐδὲ λίθος δύναται.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.311: ὠκείαις ἐλάφοισι κύων ἰσάμιλλα
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ὠκείαις ἐλάφοισι κύων ἰσάμιλλα δραμοῦσα
ἔγκυος ἡλκώθη παιδοπόρον γένεσιν
πᾶσα δὲ συγκατέμυσε κατουλωθεῖσα χρόνοισιν,
ἤδη δʼ ἡ τοκετῶν ὥριος ἦν βάσανος·
πολλὰ δʼ ἐπωρύουσαν ἀνὴρ ἐσιδηροτόμησεν,
καὶ σκύλακες φίλιοι νηδύος ἐξέθορον.
Ἀρτέμιδος λέλυται λοχίων χάρις· ἔμπαλι δʼ Ἄρης
ἦρκται μαιοῦσθαι γαστέρα θηλυτέραις,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.416: ἡ ναῦς ἀπʼ ἔργων
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ἡ ναῦς ἀπʼ ἔργων Κύπριδος γομφουμένη,
πρὸς τὸν γενάρχην πόντον ἤλυθον θεοῦ·
ἀνὴρ γὰρ ὥρης μʼ ἔμπορος τεκτήνατο,
καλέσας Ἑταίρην εἰμὶ γὰρ πᾶσιν φίλη.
ἔμβαινε θαρρῶν μισθὸν οὐκ αἰτῶ βαρύν.
ἐλθόντα δέχομαι πάντα· βαστάζω ξένον
ἀστὸν τʼ· ἐπὶ γαίης κἠν βυθῷ μʼ ἐρέσσετε.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.438: Βωλοτόμοι μύρμηκες, ὁ γῆς
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Βωλοτόμοι μύρμηκες, ὁ γῆς στρατός, ἡνίκʼ ἔτενδε
γειομόρου μελιχρὴν σμηνοδόκου χάριτα,
μηνίσας ὁ πρέσβυς, ἐς ὕδατα κρωσσὸν ἔβαψεν,
ἐνθάδε τοὺς ἀπὸ γῆς οὐ δοκέων πελάσειν.
οἱ δὲ νέας κάρφας ἀχυρίτιδας ἀντιφέροντες,
αὐτοκυβερνῆται πρὸς κύτος ἐτρόχασαν.
ἦ ῥα φίλη γαστὴρ καὶ βαιοτάτους ἀνέπεισεν
ἐκ χθονὸς εἰς Νύμφας καινοτάτους ἐρέτας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.543: Θεσσαλίης εὔιππος ὁ ταυρελάτης
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Θεσσαλίης εὔιππος ὁ ταυρελάτης χορὸς ἀνδρῶν,
χερσὶν ἀτευχήτοις θηρσὶν ὁπλιζόμενος,
κεντροτυπεῖς πώλους ζεῦξε σκιρτήματι ταύρων,
ἀμφιβαλεῖν σπεύδων πλέγμα μετωπίδιον·
ἀκρότατον δʼ ἐς γῆν κλίνας ἅμα κεὔροπον ἅμμα
θηρὸς τὴν τόσσην ἐξεκύλισε βίην.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.561: τίς σε πάγος δυσέρημος,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
τίς σε πάγος δυσέρημος, ἀνήλιος, ἐξέθρεψεν
Βορραίου Σκυθίης, ἄμπελον ἀγριάδα;
ἢ Κελτῶν νιφοβλῆτες ἀεὶ κρυμώδεες Ἄλπεις,
τῆς τε σιδηροτόκου βῶλος Ἰβηριάδος;
ἣ τοὺς ὀμφακόραγας ἐγείναο, τοὺς ἀπεπάντους
βότρυας, οἳ στυφελὴν ἐξέχεον σταγόνα.
δίζημαι, Λυκόεργε, τεὰς χέρας, ὡς ἀπὸ ῥίζης
κλήματος ὠμοτόκου βλαστὸν ὅλον θερίσῃς.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.575: οὐρανὸς ἄστρα τάχιον ἀποσβέσει,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
οὐρανὸς ἄστρα τάχιον ἀποσβέσει, ἢ τάχα νυκτὸς
ἠέλιος φαιδρὴν ὄψιν ἀπεργάσεται,
καὶ γλυκὺ νᾶμα θάλασσα βροτοῖς ἀρυτήσιμον ἕξει,
καὶ νέκυς εἰς ζωῶν χῶρον ἀναδράμεται,
ἤ ποτε Μαιονίδαο βαθυκλεὲς οὔνομʼ Ὁμήρου
λήθη γηραλέων ἁρπάσεται σελίδων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.708: ἔζευξʼ Ἑλλήσποντον ὁ βάρβαρος
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ἔζευξʼ Ἑλλήσποντον ὁ βάρβαρος ἄφρονι τόλμῃ,
τοὺς δὲ τόσους καμάτους πάντας ἔλυσε χρόνος·
ἀλλὰ Δικαιάρχεια διηπείρωσε θάλασσαν,
καὶ βυθὸν εἰς χέρσου σχῆμα μετεπλάσατο·
λᾶα, βαθὺ στήριγμα, κατερρίζωσε πέλωρον,
χερσὶ Γιγαντείαις δʼ ἔστασε νέρθεν ὕδωρ.
ἦν ἅλʼ ἀεὶ πλώειν διοδευομένη δʼ ὑπὸ ναύταις
ἄστατος, εἰς πεζοὺς ὡμολόγησε μένειν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.709: Εὐρώταν ὡς ἄρτι διάβροχον
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Εὐρώταν ὡς ἄρτι διάβροχον ἔν τε ῥεέθροις
εἵλκυσ’ ὁ τεχνίτης ἐν πυρὶ λουσάμενον
πᾶσι γὰρ ἐν κώλοις ὑδατούμενος ἀμφινένευκεν
ἐκ κορυφῆς ἐς ἄκρους ὑγροβατῶν ὄνυχας.
ἁ δὲ τέχνα ποταμῷ συνεπήρικεν· ἆ τίς ὁ πείσας
χαλκὸν κωμάζειν ὕδατος ὑγρότερον;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.742: ἄπαιρέ μου τένοντος, ὦ
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ἄπαιρέ μου τένοντος, ὦ γεωπόνε,
λέπαδνα, καὶ σίδαρον αὐλακεργάταν·
χαλκὸν γὰρ ἁμῶν οὐκ ἐσάρκωσεν Μύρων,
τέχνα δὲ ζωπόνησεν ὄψιν ἔμπνοον,
ὡς πολλάκις με κἀπομυκᾶσθαι θέλειν·
εἰς ἔργα δʼ οὐκ εἴασε, προσδήσας βάσει.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.777: ἴδʼ ὡς ὁ πῶλος
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ἴδʼ ὡς ὁ πῶλος χαλκοδαιδάλῳ τέχνᾳ
κορωνιῶν ἕστηκε· δριμὺ γὰρ βλέπων
ὑψαυχενίζει, καὶ διηνεμωμένας
κορυφῆς ἐθείρας οὐρίωκεν ἐς δρόμον.
δοκέω, χαλινοὺς εἴ τις ἡνιοστρόφος
ἐναρμόσῃ γένυσσι κἀπικεντρίσᾐ,
ὁ σὸς πόνος, Λύσιππε, καὶ παρʼ ἐλπίδας
τάχʼ ἐκδραμεῖται· τᾷ τέχνᾳ γὰρ ἐμπνέει·

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.778: γαῖαν τὴν φερέκαρπον ὅσην
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
γαῖαν τὴν φερέκαρπον ὅσην ἔζωσε περίχθων
ὠκεανὸς μεγάλῳ Καίσαρι πειθομένην,
καὶ γλαυκήν με θάλασσαν ἀπηκριβώσατο Καρπὼ
κερκίσιν ἱστοπόνοις πάντʼ ἀπομαξαμένη·
Καίσαρι δʼ † ακείνου χάρις ἤλθομεν ἦν γὰρ ἀνάσσης
δῶρα φέρειν τὰ θεοῖς καὶ πρὶν ὀφειλόμενα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.33: λάθριον ἑρπηστὴν σκολιὸν πόδα,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
λάθριον ἑρπηστὴν σκολιὸν πόδα, κισσέ, χορεύσας,
ἄγχεις τὴν Βρομίου βοτρυόπαιδα χάριν
δεσμεῖς δʼ οὐχ ἡμᾶς, ὀλέκεις δὲ σέ· τίς γὰρ ἕλοιτʼ ἂν
κισσὸν ἐπὶ κροτάφοις, μὴ κεράσας Βρόμιον;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.36: ἡνίκα μὲν καλὸς ἦς,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ἡνίκα μὲν καλὸς ἦς, Ἀρχέστρατε, κἀμφὶ παρειαῖς
οἰνωπαῖς ψυχὰς ἔφλεγες ἠιθέων,
ἡμετέρης φιλίης οὐδεὶς λόγος· ἀλλὰ μετʼ ἄλλων
παίζων, τὴν ἀκμὴν ὡς ῥόδον ἠφάνισας.
ὡς δʼ ἐπιπερκάζεις μιαρῇ τριχί, νῦν φίλον ἕλκων,
τὴν καλάμην δωρῇ, δοὺς ἑτέροις τὸ θέρος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.173: εἰ τὸ μὲν ἐκδεδάνεικας,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
εἰ τὸ μὲν ἐκδεδάνεικας, ὃ δʼ ἄρτι δίδως, ὃ δὲ μέλλεις,
οὐδέποτʼ εἶ τοῦ σοῦ κύριος ἀργυρίου.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.321: γραμματικοὶ Μώμου στυγίου τέκνα,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
γραμματικοὶ Μώμου στυγίου τέκνα, σῆτες ἀκανθῶν,
τελχῖνες βίβλων, Ζηνοδότου σκύλακες,
Καλλιμάχου στρατιῶται, ὃν ὡς ὅπλον ἐκτανύσαντες,
οὐδʼ αὐτοῦ κείνου γλῶσσαν ἀποστρέφετε,
συνδέσμων λυγρῶν θηρήτορες, οἷς τὸ μὶν ἢ
εὔαδε, καὶ ζητεῖν εἰ κύνας εἶχε Κύκλωψ,
τρίβοισθʼ εἰς αἰῶνα κατατρύζοντες ἀλιτροὶ
ἄλλων ἐς δʼ ἡμᾶς ἰὸν ἀποσβέσατε.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.347: Χαίροιθʼ οἱ περὶ κόσμον
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Χαίροιθʼ οἱ περὶ κόσμον ἀεὶ πεπλανηκότες ὄμμα,
οἳ τʼ ἀπʼ Ἀριστάρχου σῆτες ἀκανθολόγοι.
ποῖ γὰρ ἐμοὶ ζητεῖν, τίνας ἔδραμεν ἥλιος οἴμους,
καὶ τίνος ἦν Πρωτεὺς, καὶ τίς ὁ Πυγμαλίων;
γινώσκοιμʼ ὅσα λευκὸν ἔχει στίχον ἡ δὲ μέλαινα
ἱστορίη τήκοι τοὺς Περικαλλιμάχους.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XIII.1: Ἰίαίρβ θεὰ Παφίη· σὴν
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Ἰίαίρβ θεὰ Παφίη· σὴν γὰ̆ ἀεὶ δύναμιν
κάλλος τʼ ἀθάνατον καὶ σέβας ἰμβρόβν
πάντες τιμῶσιν θνατοὶ ἐφαμέριοι
ἐν πᾶσιν μύθοις ἔργοισίν τε καλοῖς·
πάντῃ γὰρ πᾶσιν σὴν δηλοῖς τιμήν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.25: τὸν ἐκ Σινώπης εἰ
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
τὸν ἐκ Σινώπης εἰ κλύεις Δαμόστρατον,
πίτυν λαβόντα τὴν κατʼ Ἰσθμὸν ἑξάκις,
τοῦτον δέδορκας· οὗ κατʼ εὔγυρον πάλην
ψάμμον πεσόντος νῶτον οὐκ ἐσφράγισεν.
ἴδʼ ἐς πρόσωπον θηρόθυμον, ὡς ἔτι
σῴζει παλαιὰν τὰν ὑπὲρ νίκας ἔριν.
λέγει δʼ ὁ χαλκός· “ἁ βάσις με λυσάτω
χὠς ἔμπνοος νῦν ἕβδομον κονίσομαι”

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.52: ἴσως με λεύσσων, ξεῖνε,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ἴσως με λεύσσων, ξεῖνε, ταυρογάστορα
καὶ στερρόγυιον, ὡς Ἄτλαντα δεύτερον,
θαμβεῖς, ἀπιστῶν εἰ βρότειος ἡ φύσις.
ἀλλʼ ἴσθι μʼ Ἡρᾶν Λαδικῆα πάμμαχον,
ὃν Σμύρνα καὶ δρῦς Περγάμου κατέστεφεν,
Δελφοί, Κόρινθος, Ἦλις, Ἄργος, Ἄκτιον
λοιπῶν δʼ ἀέθλων ἢν ἐρευνήσῃς κράτος,
καὶ τὴν Λίβυσσαν ἐξαριθμήσεις κόνιν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.81: ἢ θεὸς ἦλθʼ ἐπὶ
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ἢ θεὸς ἦλθʼ ἐπὶ γῆν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ, εἰκόνα δείξων,
Φειδία· ἢ σὺ γʼ ἔβης τὸν θεὸν ὀψόμενος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.93: ὤλεσα τὸν Νεμέας θῆρʼ
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ὤλεσα τὸν Νεμέας θῆρʼ ἄπλετον, ὤλεσα δʼ ὕδρην
καὶ ταῦρον, κάπρου δʼ ἀμφετίναξα γένυν
ζωστῆρʼ ἑλκύσσας, πώλους Διομήδεος εἷλον
χρύσεα μᾶλα κλάσας, Γηρυόνην ἔλαβον
Αὐγείας μʼ ἐδάη· κεμὰς οὐ φύγεν ἔκτανον ὄρνις·
Κέρβερον ἠγαγόμην αὐτὸς Ὄλυμπον ἔχω.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.104: Ἥρη τοῦτʼ ἄρα λοιπὸν
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Ἥρη τοῦτʼ ἄρα λοιπὸν ἐβούλετο πᾶσιν ἐπʼ ἄθλοις,
ὅπλων γυμνὸν ἰδεῖν τὸν θρασὺν Ἡρακλέα.
ποῦ χλαίνωμα λέοντος, ὃ τʼ εὐροίζητος ἐπʼ ὤμοις
ἰός, καὶ βαρύπους ὄζος ὁ θηρολέτης;
πάντα σ’ Ἔρως ἀπέδυσε· καὶ οὐ ξένον, εἰ Δία κύκνον
ποιήσας, ὅπλων νοσφίσαθʼ Ἡρακλέα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.137: τίς σοῦ, Κολχὶς ἄθεσμε,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.141: Κολχίδα, τὴν ἐπὶ παισὶν
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Κολχίδα, τὴν ἐπὶ παισὶν ἀλάστορα, τραυλὲ χελιδών,
πῶς ἔτλης τεκέων μαῖαν ἔχειν ἰδίων;
ἧς ἔτι κανθὸς ὕφαιμος ἀπαστράπτει φόνιον πῦρ,
καὶ πολιὸς γενύων ἀφρὸς ἄπο σταλάει·
ἀρτιβρεχὴς δὲ σίδηρος ἐφʼ αἵματι. φεῦγε πανώλη
μητέρα, κἀν κηρῷ τεκνοφονοῦσαν ἔτι.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.177: Κύπρι φιλομμειδής, θαλαμηπόλε, τίς
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.193: κράμβης ἅψωμαι, Κυλλήνιε; μή,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
κράμβης ἅψωμαι, Κυλλήνιε; μή, παροδῖτα.
τίς φθόνος ἐκ λαχάνων; οὐ φθόνος, ἀλλὰ νόμος,
ἀλλοτρίων ἀπέχειν κλοπίμους χέρας. ὢ παραδόξου·
μὴ κλέπτειν Ἑρμῆς καινὸν ἔθηκε νόμον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.215: συλήσαντες Ὄλυμπον ἴδʼ ὡς
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
συλήσαντες Ὄλυμπον ἴδʼ ὡς ὅπλοισιν Ἔρωτες
κοσμοῦντʼ ἀθανάτων, σκῦλα φρυασσόμενοι.
Φοίβου τόξα φέρουσι, Διὸς δὲ κεραυνόν,Ἄρηος
ὅπλον καὶ κυνέην, Ἡρακλέους ῥόπαλον,
ῥόπαλον τε θεοῦ τριβελὲς δόρυ, θύρσα τε Βάκχου,
πτηνὰ πέδιλʼ Ἑρμοῦ, λαμπάδας Ἀρτέμιδος.
οὐκ ἄχθος θνητοῖς εἴκειν βελέεσσιν ἐρώτων,
δαίμονες οἷς ὅπλων κόσμον ἔδωκαν ἔχειν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.240: ὡραίας γʼ ἐσορῶ τὰς
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ὡραίας γʼ ἐσορῶ τὰς ἰσχάδας· εἴ γε λαβεῖν μοι
συγχωρεῖς ὀλίγας. θίγγανε μηδεμιᾶς.
ὀργίλος ὡς ὁ Πρίηπος. † ἐρεῖς ἔτι καὶ κενὸς ἥξεις.
ναὶ λίτομαι. δός μοι· καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ δέομαι.
χρῄζεις γάρ, λέγε μοι, παρʼ ἐμοῦ τινος; ἔστι νόμος που·
δὸς λάβε. καὶ θεὸς ὢν ἀργυρίου σὺ
ἄλλο τι χρῆμα φιλῶ. ποῖον τόδε; τἀμὰ κατέσθων
σῦκα, δὸς εὐθύμως ἰσχάδα τὴν ὀπίσω.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.203: ἡ γρῆϋς ἡ χερνῆτις,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
ἡ γρῆϋς ἡ χερνῆτις, ἡ γυιὴ πόδας,
πύστιν κατʼ ἐσθλὴν ὕδατος παιωνίου ,
ἦλθέν ποθερπύζουσα σὺν δρυὸς ξύλῳ,
τό μιν διεσκήριπτε τὴν τετρωμένην·
οἶκτος δὲ Νύμφας εἷλεν, αἵτʼ ἐριβρόμου
Αἴτνης παρωρείῃσι Συμαίθου πατρὸς
ἔχουσι δινήεντος ὑγρὸν οἰκίον.
καὶ τῆς μὲν ἀμφίχωλον ἀρτεμὲς σκέλος
θερμὴ διεστήριξεν Αἰτναίη λιβάς·
νύμφαις δʼ ἔλειπε βάκτρον, αἵτʼ ἐπῄνεσαν
πέμπειν μιν ἀστήρικτον, ἡσθείσαις δόσει.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.692: γλύκων, τὸ Περγαμηνὸν Ἀσίδι
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
γλύκων, τὸ Περγαμηνὸν Ἀσίδι κλέος,
ὁ παμμάχων κεραυνός, ὁ πλατὺς πόδας,
ὁ καινὸς Ἄτλας, αἳ τʼ ἀνίκατοι χέρες
ἔρροντι· τὸν δὲ πρόσθεν οὔτʼ ἐν Ἰταλοῖς,
οὔθʼ Ἑλλάδι προωστόν, οὔτʼ ἐν Ἀσίδι,
ὁ πάντα νικῶν Ἀίδης ἀνέτραπεν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.264: θάμνου ποτʼ ἄκρους ἀμφὶ
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
θάμνου ποτʼ ἄκρους ἀμφὶ κλῶνας ἥμενος
τέττιξ πτερῷ, φλέγοντος ἡλίου μέσου,
νηδὺν ῥαπίζων, δαίδαλʼ αὐτουργῷ μέλει
ἡδὺς κατωργάνιζε τῆς ἐρημίας.
Κρίτων δʼ, ὁ πάσης ἰξοεργὸς Πιαλεὺς
θήρης, ἀσάρκου νῶτα δουνακεύσατο.
τίσιν δʼ ἔτισεν εἰς γὰρ ἠθάδας πάγας
σφαλεὶς ἀλᾶται παντὸς ἱμείρων πτεροῦ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.265: Ἰοτυπὴς Διὸς ὄρνις ἐτίσατο
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Ἰοτυπὴς Διὸς ὄρνις ἐτίσατο Κρῆτα φαρέτρης,
οὐρανόθεν τόξῳ τόξον ἀμυνόμενος·
κεῖνον δʼ εὐθὺς ἄκοντι παλινδρομέοντι κατέκτα
ἠέριος, πίπτων δʼ ἔκτανεν ὡς ἔθανεν.
μηκέτʼ ἐφʼ ὑμετέροις ἀψευδέσι Κρῆτες ὀιστοῖς
αὐχεῖθʼ· ὑμνείσθω καὶ Διὸς εὐστοχίη.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.26b: Ἄφλοιος καὶ ἄφυλλος, ὁδοίπορε,
poems.author: Philippus of Thessalonica
poems.text:
Ἄφλοιος καὶ ἄφυλλος, ὁδοίπορε, τῷδʼ ἐπὶ νώτῳ
Ἀλκαίῳ σταυρὸς πήγνυται ἡλίβατος.
